docs.text:

Simple meanings of the technical terms used in this knowledge base, in A–Z order. Use the search box at the top to find a term quickly.

Term Simple meaning Learn more 4G camera A camera that sends video over a mobile SIM network. Used where there's no wired internet, e.g. construction sites. AI use cases by customer type Active deterrence Cameras with a built-in siren, speaker or flashing light that scare intruders away, not just record them. Intrusion, line-crossing and loitering AcuSense Hikvision's entry AI range: person and vehicle filtering on cameras and recorders. AI product lines AHD / HDCVI / HD-TVI Different types of analog HD camera technology. Different brands use different types. "Turbo HD" is one brand's name for HD-TVI. Adding AI to existing cameras AI box A separate device that reads video from existing cameras or recorders, runs AI and sends alerts. Nothing else needs replacing. Adding AI to existing cameras AI camera A camera with an AI chip inside that recognises people, vehicles and so on. Also called edge AI. What makes a camera "AI" AI chip A small processor inside a camera or recorder, built specially to run AI. What makes a camera "AI" AI model The program that recognises objects, trained on millions of photos. What makes a camera "AI" AI NVR An NVR (recorder for IP cameras) with an AI chip that adds AI to normal cameras. Where the AI runs Allow list A list of known people or vehicles (employees, residents, VIPs). A match can open a gate or send a welcome alert. Face recognition, ANPR AMC Annual Maintenance Contract. A yearly service fee the customer pays for maintenance and support. Where the AI runs Analog camera An older type of CCTV camera that uses coaxial cable and connects to a DVR. Adding AI to existing cameras ANPR / LPR Automatic Number Plate Recognition (also License Plate Recognition). The camera reads vehicle number plates automatically. ANPR Battery optimisation A phone setting that stops apps running in the background. A common reason CCTV alerts don't arrive. Why AI fails Block list A list of people or vehicles to watch out for (known shoplifters, banned vehicles). A match sends an alert. Face recognition, ANPR BOM Bill of Materials. The list of all items and quantities in a quote. Pricing, packages and AMC Boom barrier The motorised gate arm at a vehicle entrance. Can open automatically with ANPR. AI use cases by customer type Channel One camera input on a recorder. A 16-channel NVR can connect 16 cameras. AI may work on only some channels. Where the AI runs Cloud AI AI that runs on internet servers instead of on site. Usually has a monthly fee and needs good internet. Where the AI runs Coaxial cable The round cable with a metal pin at the end, used by analog cameras. Adding AI to existing cameras ColorVu Hikvision's colour night vision range. Not AI by itself; often combined with AcuSense. AI product lines Comprehensive AMC An AMC that covers service, labour and replacement parts. Pricing, packages and AMC Confidence score How sure the AI is about what it sees, e.g. "Person: 92%." How AI detects people and vehicles Conversion rate The share of visitors who buy. Bills ÷ visitors, e.g. 100 ÷ 500 = 20%. People counting Deep learning The type of AI used in modern cameras. On a spec sheet, a sign of real AI. Reading a spec sheet DeepinMind Hikvision's AI NVR range with face recognition and smart search. AI product lines DeepinView Hikvision's advanced AI camera range: face recognition, ANPR, counting. AI product lines Detection The AI finding an object and drawing a box around it, e.g. "a person is here." How AI detects people and vehicles Detection zone The area you draw on the camera screen where the AI should look. Leave out trees and roads to avoid false alarms. How AI detects people and vehicles DORI A standard for how much detail a camera captures at a distance: Detect, Observe, Recognise, Identify. Camera placement for AI DPDP Act India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act. It protects personal data such as faces. Needs signage, consent and secure storage. Face recognition DVR Digital Video Recorder. Records video from analog cameras. Adding AI to existing cameras Edge AI AI that runs inside the camera itself ("at the edge"). Same as an AI camera. Where the AI runs Enrolment Uploading clear photos of people into a face recognition system. Face recognition Face capture The camera only takes photos of faces. Recognising who it is needs an AI NVR or software. Reading a spec sheet Face detection Knowing that a face is there, without knowing whose it is. Face recognition Face recognition Identifying who a person is by matching their face with an enrolled list. Face recognition Faceprint A number code made from the shape of a face, like a fingerprint for faces. Face recognition False alarm An alert for something that isn't a threat, e.g. a dog reported as a person. How AI detects people and vehicles Firmware The software built into a camera or recorder. Updates fix bugs and improve features. Why AI fails Footfall The number of people who visit a place. People counting Frame A single picture in a video. Video is many frames per second, like a flipbook. How AI detects people and vehicles H.265 A video compression format that saves hard disk space. Reading a spec sheet Heatmap A coloured map showing where people go or stand most. People counting HSRP High Security Registration Plate. India's standard number plate with a standard font, easier for ANPR to read. ANPR Hybrid system A system that combines AI cameras, an AI NVR and/or cloud, each doing a different job. Where the AI runs IK10 Vandal-proof rating: strong against hits. Reading a spec sheet Intrusion detection An alert when a person or vehicle enters a zone you've drawn. Intrusion, line-crossing and loitering IP camera A network camera that uses a LAN cable and connects to an NVR. Adding AI to existing cameras IP67 Dust- and water-proof rating, needed for outdoor cameras. Reading a spec sheet IR (infrared) Invisible light used for night vision. When IR fails, night images go dark. ANPR IR reflection IR light bouncing off a nearby wall, roof edge or pole, making the picture white or foggy. Camera placement for AI Lens (focal length) Sets how wide or far a camera sees. 2.8 mm = wide but short; 6–8 mm = narrow but further. Camera placement for AI Line-crossing An alert when a person or vehicle crosses a line you've drawn, in a chosen direction. Intrusion, line-crossing and loitering Loitering An alert when a person stays in a zone longer than a set time. Intrusion, line-crossing and loitering Missed event When the AI fails to alert for something real, e.g. an intruder. How AI detects people and vehicles Non-comprehensive AMC An AMC that covers service and labour; parts are charged extra. Pricing, packages and AMC NVR Network Video Recorder. Records video from IP cameras. Where the AI runs Occupancy How many people are inside right now (people in − people out). People counting OCR Optical Character Recognition. Reading text, such as a number plate, from an image. ANPR ONVIF A common "language" that lets cameras and recorders from different brands work together. Recording usually works across brands; AI features may not. Adding AI to existing cameras Overhead counting camera A ceiling camera looking straight down at an entrance, made for accurate people counting. People counting Payback period How many months a system takes to pay for itself: price ÷ monthly saving. Pricing, packages and AMC Pixels per metre How many tiny dots cover 1 metre of the scene. More = more detail. Camera placement for AI PoE Power over Ethernet. One network cable carries both video and power to an IP camera. Adding AI to existing cameras PPE detection AI that checks if workers wear safety gear (Personal Protective Equipment) such as helmets and vests. AI use cases by customer type Schedule The times when alerts are switched on, e.g. 10pm–7am only. Intrusion, line-crossing and loitering Sensitivity / threshold The setting that decides how sure the AI must be before alerting. Too high = false alarms; too low = missed events. How AI detects people and vehicles Shutter speed How fast the camera captures each picture. Fast shutter stops moving vehicles from looking blurry. ANPR Smart search Finding people or vehicles in recordings by colour, type and time, in minutes instead of hours. Smart search Solar camera A camera powered by a solar panel and battery. Used where there's no power supply. AI use cases by customer type Spec sheet / datasheet The PDF listing exactly what a product can do. Why AI fails Varifocal lens A lens whose zoom can be adjusted at installation (motorised versions adjust remotely). Camera placement for AI VCA Video Content Analytics. A spec sheet heading for smart or AI features. Reading a spec sheet WDR Wide Dynamic Range. Handles bright and dark areas in the same picture, e.g. a sunny doorway. Reading a spec sheet WizMind Dahua's advanced AI range: face recognition, counting, ANPR, detailed search. docs.title: Number-plate reading (ANPR)
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-10

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: ANPR (Automatic Number Plate Recognition, also called LPR) reads vehicle number plates automatically to log vehicles, open gates for known vehicles, or alert on banned ones.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: It replaces the paper register at the gate, speeds up entry for residents and employees, and gives a searchable record of every vehicle with photo, date and time.

docs.title: How it works (simple)
docs.text:
1. Spot the vehicle: the AI detects a car, bike or truck.
  2. Find the plate on the vehicle.
  3. Read the characters (OCR), e.g. MH 12 AB 1234.
  4. Check the list and act: log it, alert the guard, or open the boom barrier.
flowchart LR
    A[Vehicle arrives] --> B[Find the plate]
    B --> C["Read characters<br/>MH 12 AB 1234"]
    C --> D{Check lists}
    D -- Allow list --> E[Open barrier]
    D -- Block list --> F[Alert guard]
    D -- Not on any list --> G["Log it, guard<br/>approves entry"]

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
Use What happens Allow list A resident's or employee's vehicle arrives and the barrier opens automatically Block list A banned or suspicious vehicle arrives and the guard gets an alert Entry and exit log Number, photo, date and time saved for every vehicle Truck tracking Know when each truck came in, went out and how long it stayed Parking Track parking time for billing or overstay alerts

Best customers: housing societies, factories, warehouses, logistics parks, hospitals, malls, schools, office campuses.

docs.title: India-specific challenges
docs.text:
Problem Example Fancy or non-standard fonts Designer plates, stickers Dirty, faded or broken plates Mud, dust, bent plates Two-line plates Bikes, autos, trucks Hand-painted truck plates Painted on the body, often worn Different plate colours White (private), yellow (commercial), green (EV), black (rental)

Newer HSRP plates (High Security Registration Plates) use a standard font and are much easier to read.

docs.title: Setup tips
docs.text:
1. Use a dedicated ANPR camera. A normal wide camera covering the whole gate can't read plates reliably.
  2. Install at a slow point: a gate, barrier or speed breaker, not an open road.
  3. Keep the angle small: face the plate as straight as possible.
  4. One lane per camera (in-lane and out-lane = 2 cameras).
  5. Follow the camera's recommended distance, so the plate is big enough on screen.
  6. For night, use cameras with IR light and fast shutter speed to avoid headlight glare and motion blur.

docs.title: How accurate is it?
docs.text:
• Controlled gate (slow vehicles, good angle, clean HSRP plates): very accurate.
  • Open roads, speeding vehicles, dirty or fancy plates, bad angles: accuracy drops a lot.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Promising plate reading from an existing wide gate camera.
  • Installing where vehicles pass at speed.
  • One camera trying to cover two lanes.
  • Promising 100% accuracy. Muddy or fancy plates may need a manual check.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A 400-flat housing society replaced its paper register with 2 ANPR cameras (in-lane and out-lane) at the boom barrier, with a speed breaker before it. Residents' vehicles open the barrier automatically, visitors are captured with a photo and approved by the guard, and banned vehicles trigger an alert. The committee can search records in seconds.

Upsell: ANPR + boom barrier + monthly AMC.

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "The camera reads every vehicle number automatically. Residents' cars open the gate by themselves, visitors get logged with a photo and time, and you can search any vehicle in seconds. No more paper register. It works best at the gate where vehicles slow down."

docs.title: Face recognition
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-10

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: Face recognition identifies who a person is by comparing their face with a list of enrolled people. It only works with a close, front-facing, well-lit view of the face.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: It can alert the owner when a VIP, an employee, a known shoplifter or a stranger arrives. It's also the feature most often oversold, so setting the right expectations avoids unhappy customers.

docs.title: Face detection vs face recognition
docs.text: What it means Example Face detection "There's a face here" "A person entered" Face recognition "This is Ramesh" "Ramesh (employee) entered at 9:02 am"

docs.title: How it works (simple)
docs.text:
1. Enrol: upload clear photos of people into the system.
  2. Faceprint: the system turns each face into a unique number code (distance between the eyes, shape of the nose and jaw).
  3. Compare: each new face is compared with the enrolled list.
  4. Match score: e.g. "Ramesh, 94% match." Above the threshold = a match.
flowchart LR
    A[Enrol clear photos] --> B["Faceprint<br/>number code"]
    C[Person walks past] --> D[Faceprint of the new face]
    B --> E{Compare}
    D --> E
    E -- "Match above threshold" --> F["Name + alert<br/>e.g. VIP arrived"]
    E -- No match --> G[Stranger]

docs.title: Types of lists
docs.text:
• Allow list: employees, family, VIP customers
  • Block list: known shoplifters or banned people
  • Stranger alert: anyone not on the allow list

docs.title: When to use it / when not to
docs.text: Good for Not good for Office or factory attendance and door access Wide cameras covering a whole gate or compound VIP and shoplifter alerts at a showroom entrance Cameras mounted high, looking down Stranger alerts at a home door or pedestrian gate Places where people wear helmets or masks Narrow entry points: doors, turnstiles, corridors Crowded areas with fast-moving people

docs.title: Setup tips
docs.text:
• Use a dedicated face recognition camera. A normal wide camera is not a face recognition camera.
  • Install it at a narrow point (door, turnstile, corridor) at about head height, facing people as they walk in.
  • Avoid backlight, e.g. a bright doorway behind the person.
  • Use clear, recent, front-facing photos for enrolment.

docs.title: Why it fails
docs.text: Problem Why Too far away The face is too small to measure Side angle or from above It needs the face nearly straight on Mask, helmet, cap, sunglasses Key parts of the face are hidden Backlight The face appears dark Crowds Faces overlap and move fast Poor enrolment photos Weak faceprint

docs.title: Privacy and legal
docs.text:
• A face is personal data, protected under India's DPDP Act.
  • Put up clear signage that cameras and face recognition are in use.
  • Get consent from employees for attendance or access systems.
  • Keep the data secure, limit access, and don't keep it longer than needed.
  • For public spaces, schools or large-scale use, the customer should take legal advice.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Promising face recognition from an existing gate or wall camera.
  • Installing the face camera too high or at a side angle.
  • Skipping signage and consent.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
• Works: a jewellery showroom puts a face recognition camera above the entrance door at head height, with a block list of known shoplifters and an allow list of VIP customers. The manager gets alerts like "VIP: Mr. Sharma has arrived."
  • Doesn't work: a housing society wants face recognition from a 4th-floor camera covering the whole main gate. Faces are too small, seen from above, and many people wear helmets. Better: number-plate reading for vehicles at the main gate, plus a face recognition camera at the pedestrian gate.

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "Face recognition can tell you exactly who walked in, like a VIP customer or a known shoplifter. But it needs a special camera at the door, at face height, where people walk straight towards it. A far or high camera can't do it, so we'll place it where it actually works."

docs.title: Intrusion, line-crossing and loitering
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-10

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: You draw a zone or a line on the camera's screen, and the AI alerts when a person or vehicle enters, crosses or stays too long, while ignoring animals, trees and rain.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: These are the features customers buy most. They warn the owner about intruders while it's happening, and with a siren or light they can scare intruders away before anything is stolen.

docs.title: How it works (simple)
docs.text: Feature What you draw Alerts when… Like… Intrusion A zone (box) Someone enters it An invisible "no entry" carpet Line-crossing A line Someone crosses it, in the chosen direction (A→B, B→A or both) An invisible laser beam Loitering A zone + a time limit Someone stays longer than the limit A shopkeeper who notices someone standing outside too long

docs.title: When to use each
docs.text:
Feature Good for Intrusion Warehouse yards, godowns, rooftops, server or store rooms Line-crossing Tops of boundary walls, gates after closing, one-way entries and exits Loitering Shopfronts after closing, ATMs, cash counters, parking, back lanes, outside school gates

Loitering is useful because thieves often check out a place first. It can warn the owner before anything happens.

docs.title: Setup tips
docs.text:
1. Schedule: turn alerts on only when the place is closed (e.g. 10pm–7am). Otherwise staff trigger alerts all day.
  2. Target type: choose person, vehicle or both. Wall = person only. Gate after hours = both.
  3. Intrusion delay: where available, require someone to be inside the zone for a few seconds (e.g. 2–3 s) before alerting.
  4. Line direction: set the direction to match the threat, e.g. outside → inside for a wall.
  5. Actions on alert: phone notification, siren or voice warning, flashing light, recording, NVR alarm.

docs.title: Active deterrence cameras
docs.text: Cameras with a built-in speaker and flashing light can warn intruders automatically ("You are in a restricted area"). They don't just record the thief, they scare him away. This is a strong selling point.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No schedule: alerts fire all day from staff, and the customer turns them off.
  • Wrong target type: vehicle alerts on a wall where only people matter, causing extra alerts.
  • Line drawn in both directions when only one direction matters, which doubles the alerts.
  • Zones that include trees or a public road, which cause unnecessary alerts.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A textile godown had small thefts at night through the back wall. The setup:

  • Line-crossing on the back wall (outside → inside, person only)
  • Intrusion on the loading yard (10pm–7am)
  • Loitering in the back lane (alert after 2 minutes)
  • Cameras with siren and flashing light

When someone climbed the wall, the camera flashed and played a warning, the owner got a phone alert with a clip, and the person ran away before taking anything.

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "Normal CCTV shows you the theft the next morning. With AI, we draw an invisible line on your wall. If anyone crosses it at night, the camera sounds a warning, flashes a light and sends a video to your phone, so the thief runs away before taking anything."

docs.title: People counting
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-10

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: The camera counts people going in and out through a line at the entrance, turning CCTV into business reports: footfall, peak hours, occupancy and conversion rate.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: It helps owners run the business better, not just protect it. This is how to sell AI CCTV to customers who say "I don't have a theft problem."

docs.title: How it works (simple)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Virtual line at the entrance] --> B[Count IN]
    A --> C[Count OUT]
    B --> D["People inside now<br/>= IN − OUT"]
    C --> D
    B --> E["Reports: footfall,<br/>peak hours, conversion"]

docs.title: What the owner gets
docs.text: Report What it tells them Who cares Footfall Visitors per day, week, month Shops, malls, showrooms Peak hours Busiest times of day Staff planning Occupancy People inside right now Malls, temples, event halls, offices Heatmap Where people go or stand most, shown as colours Retail product placement Queue alert Too many people waiting at billing Supermarkets, banks, hospitals

docs.title: Conversion rate
docs.text:
Number Visitors (from camera) 500 Bills (from billing software) 100 Conversion rate 100 ÷ 500 = 20%

If visitors go up but bills don't, there's a problem with staff, pricing or stock.

docs.title: Types of counting cameras
docs.text:
Overhead counting camera Normal AI camera with a counting line Mounted Ceiling, looking straight down at the entrance Wall, at an angle Accuracy High, even in crowds Good when not crowded, drops with groups Cost Higher (dedicated device) Lower (uses existing AI features) Best for Malls, busy stores, accurate reports Small shops, rough footfall numbers

For detecting intruders, a straight-down view is bad. For counting at a door, a dedicated overhead camera is best, because it's designed for that view.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Groups walking close together get counted as fewer people.
  • Trolleys, prams and kids confuse the count.
  • Very wide entrances may need 2 cameras.
  • Staff going in and out get counted too. Check whether the system can filter them out.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A clothing store saw 600 visitors on Sunday but only 60 bills (10%), compared to 25% on weekdays. The owner added 2 staff on Sundays and conversion rose to 18%. The camera paid for itself in sales.

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "This camera counts every customer who walks in. You'll know your busiest hours, how many visitors actually buy, and whether a new offer is bringing more people in, all on your phone."

docs.title: Smart search
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-10

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: Smart search finds people or vehicles in recorded footage by colour, type, time and camera, in minutes instead of hours.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: After an incident, finding the right clip by watching footage can take hours. Smart search gives results quickly, with clips ready to share with the police.

docs.title: How it works (simple)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Camera records] --> B["AI labels each person<br/>and vehicle"]
    B --> C["Labels saved<br/>with the video"]
    C --> D["You search:<br/>person + blue top + 2–4pm"]
    D --> E["Matching photos<br/>in seconds"]
    E --> F[Click to open the video]

docs.title: Normal CCTV vs smart search
docs.text: Normal CCTV AI smart search How Watch footage from every camera Choose filters or type, and get results Time 2–3 hours or more A few minutes Result Tired eyes, easy to miss Thumbnails of every match, click to jump to the video

docs.title: What you can search by
docs.text: People Vehicles Top colour, bottom colour Type: car, bike, truck, bus Bag, hat or helmet, glasses Colour Direction of movement Number plate (with ANPR) Time, camera, zone Time, camera, direction

docs.title: The newest level: type a sentence
docs.text: Newer systems, mostly cloud-based, let you type plain words, e.g. "man carrying a ladder near the back gate last night." This is still new and more expensive.

docs.title: Setup tips
docs.text:
• Usually needs AI cameras plus an AI NVR that supports it, or a cloud system.
  • Check spec sheets for "smart search", "attribute search" or "human/vehicle search".

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A phone went missing from a mobile shop counter. With 16 cameras and 8 hours of footage, a manual search would take half a day. Smart search ("person, red top, 3pm–5pm, cameras 1–4") found the person in 2 minutes, with clips ready for the police.

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "If anything goes missing, you don't need to watch hours of video. Just choose 'person, red shirt, 3 to 5pm' and the system shows you every match in a minute or two."

docs.title: How AI detects people and vehicles
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-10

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: The AI draws a box around what it recognises, gives a confidence score, and sends an alert if the score is above the threshold you set.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Video frame] --> B["AI draws a box<br/>around the object"]
    B --> C["Confidence score<br/>e.g. Person 92%"]
    C --> D{"Above the<br/>threshold?"}
    D -- Yes --> E[Send alert]
    D -- No --> F[Ignore]

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: The right settings decide whether the customer gets trustworthy alerts, too many false alarms, or missed intruders.

docs.title: How it works (simple)
docs.text:
• Frames: video is many photos per second, like a flipbook. The AI checks each one.
  • Detection: the AI draws a box around each person or vehicle it recognises.
  • Confidence score: each box shows how sure the AI is, e.g. "Person: 92%."
  • Threshold (sensitivity): the minimum score needed to send an alert.

docs.title: Setting the sensitivity
docs.text: Setting What happens Risk Too high sensitivity (low threshold) Catches everything False alarms: dogs or bags reported as people Too low sensitivity (high threshold) Very few false alarms Missed events: a real intruder goes unreported Balanced Few false alarms, few misses Needs testing at each site

docs.title: The two kinds of mistakes
docs.text:
• False alarm: the AI alerts on something that isn't a threat. This is annoying, and the customer stops trusting alerts.
  • Missed event: the AI misses a real person. This is dangerous, because it's what the customer paid to prevent.

Match the setting to what the customer cares about most. A warehouse at night usually prefers a few extra alerts over missing a thief.

docs.title: When the AI struggles
docs.text:
• The person is too far away and looks like a few dots
  • Poor light, or headlights shining into the lens
  • The person is half hidden behind a car or wall
  • The camera is too high, looking straight down, so a person looks like just a head

docs.title: Setup tips
docs.text:
• Tune the sensitivity and detection zone at every installation. AI cameras aren't "install and forget."
  • Draw detection zones to cover the area that matters (the wall, the gate) and leave out trees and roads.
  • Mount cameras at about 3–4 m and angle them to see people from the front or side, not from straight above.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Problem Wrong fix Right fix False alerts from a dog or trees Replace with a costlier camera, or turn AI off Lower sensitivity a little and redraw the detection zone Camera misses people at a gate Blame the AI chip or the internet Lower the camera and change the angle Customer asks "will it catch everyone?" Promise 100% Explain it depends on distance, light and angle

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A school's boundary-wall cameras sent 30+ alerts a night because of trees. The installer reduced sensitivity a little and redrew the zone to cover only the wall. Alerts dropped to 1–2 a night, all real.

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "The camera checks every frame and only alerts when it's confident it sees a person or vehicle. During installation we tune how sensitive it is for your site, so you get real alerts without missing anything important."

docs.text: • What makes a camera "AI"

docs.title: What makes a camera "AI"
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-10

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: A normal camera sees pixels. An AI camera understands what those pixels are: a person, a vehicle or nothing important.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: Normal cameras send so many false alerts (trees, rain, animals, headlights) that owners mute the app and miss real incidents. AI cameras send fewer alerts that they can trust.

docs.title: How it works (simple)
docs.text:
• An AI camera has a small AI chip inside it.
  • The chip runs an AI model, a program trained on millions of photos of people and vehicles.
  • Like a child who has seen many dogs, the model recognises people and vehicles it has never seen before.
  • Instead of "pixels changed," it reports what it saw and how sure it is, e.g. "person, 92% sure."

docs.title: Normal motion detection vs AI
docs.text: Normal camera AI camera What triggers an alert Any pixel change: trees, rain, shadows, animals, headlights Only people or vehicles Like a guard who… Shouts at every leaf and cat Only shouts when he sees a person or vehicle Result Owner mutes the alerts Owner trusts the alerts

docs.title: The 3 levels of AI in the market
docs.text:
1. Basic AI: a person and vehicle filter. The most common type and the easiest to sell.
  2. Advanced AI: face recognition, number-plate reading, people counting, attributes such as clothing colour or helmet.
  3. Cloud or smart search AI: search footage by typing, e.g. "man in red shirt near gate."

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: • Trusting the "AI" label. Some cameras are sold as AI but only have basic motion detection. Check the spec sheet for human/vehicle classification or similar.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A warehouse with trees, stray dogs and a busy road nearby:

  • Normal cameras: around 200 alerts a night. The owner mutes the app and misses a real theft.
  • AI cameras: 2–3 alerts a night, all real people. Every alert gets checked.

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "Motion detection only sees that something moved, so it alerts for trees, rain and dogs too. An AI camera knows the difference between a person and a dog, so it only alerts you when it really matters, and you can trust every alert."

docs.title: Where the AI runs: camera, NVR or cloud
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-10

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: The AI "brain" can be inside the camera (edge AI), inside the recorder (AI NVR), or on internet servers (cloud). This decides the cost, the features, and whether the customer can keep old cameras.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: It decides whether they must replace cameras, whether there's a monthly fee, whether they need good internet, and which features they get.

docs.title: How it works (simple)
docs.text:
Where the brain is Like… AI camera (edge AI) Inside each camera Every guard is trained and decides for himself AI NVR Inside the recorder Guards are just eyes, and one smart supervisor watches all screens Cloud AI On internet servers Guards send video to an expert team at head office 
flowchart LR
    subgraph Edge["AI camera"]
        A1[AI camera] --> A2[Normal NVR] --> A3[Alert]
    end
    subgraph NVR["AI NVR"]
        B1[Normal cameras] --> B2[AI NVR] --> B3[Alert]
    end
    subgraph Cloud["Cloud AI"]
        C1[Cameras] --> C2[Box or NVR] -- internet --> C3[Cloud AI] --> C4["Alert + dashboard"]
    end

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: AI camera AI NVR Cloud Keep old cameras? No Yes Usually (needs a box or compatible NVR) Upfront cost Medium Lowest for upgrades Low to medium Monthly fee None None Yes Needs good internet? No No Yes AI features Good Good Most advanced Multi-branch view Basic (app) Basic (app) Excellent Data stays on site? Yes Yes No Best for New installs, small and mid sites Upgrading existing sites Chains, advanced needs

docs.title: Pros and cons
docs.text:
AI camera (edge AI)

  • Works with a normal NVR in most cases, gives fast alerts, and doesn't need internet except to send phone alerts.
  • Old cameras must be replaced, and features are limited to that camera model.

AI NVR

  • The customer keeps existing cameras, and one box handles AI and smart search.
  • AI is often limited to some channels, so always check the spec sheet. If the NVR fails, AI stops for all cameras.

Cloud AI

  • The most advanced features, multi-branch dashboards and automatic updates.
  • Needs stable internet (especially upload speed), has a monthly fee, and video leaves the premises (privacy).

docs.title: Hybrid systems
docs.text: Many systems combine them: AI cameras for detection, an AI NVR for smart search and recording, and the cloud for remote and multi-branch viewing.

docs.title: Which one to choose
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Q1{"Chain with many branches<br/>and good internet?"}
    Q1 -- Yes --> C[Cloud or hybrid]
    Q1 -- No --> Q2{"Already has working<br/>cameras?"}
    Q2 -- Yes --> N[AI NVR]
    Q2 -- No --> E[AI cameras]

docs.title: Business angle
docs.text: How we earn AI camera / AI NVR One-time sale + installation + AMC Cloud One-time hardware + monthly subscription (recurring income if resold)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Customer Situation Best choice Why Small kirana shop New install, 4 cameras, basic budget AI cameras + normal NVR Simple, no monthly fee Warehouse 16 old cameras working fine, wants night intrusion alerts AI NVR Keeps cameras, adds AI at the lowest cost Pharmacy chain, 12 branches Wants all stores on one dashboard Cloud or hybrid Central view, monthly plan

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "The 'brain' that understands the video can be in the camera, in the recorder, or online. If your cameras already work, we can add an AI recorder and keep them. If you're installing new, AI cameras are best. For many branches, an online system lets you see every store from one screen."

docs.title: Adding AI to existing cameras
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-10

docs.title: In one line
docs.text:
Most customers don't need new cameras to get AI. Check whether the cameras are analog or IP and whether the image quality is good, then upgrade the "brain": an AI DVR/XVR, an AI NVR, or an AI box. Replace only the key or poor cameras.

Pitch: "Keep your cameras. Upgrade the brain."

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: They get AI alerts at a fraction of the cost of a new system, without throwing away cameras that work.

docs.title: Step 1: Analog or IP?
docs.text: Analog (HD) cameras IP cameras Cable Coaxial (round cable with a metal pin) + separate power Network cable (LAN, often PoE) Recorder DVR NVR Common at Older and budget installations Newer and mid-to-high-end installations How to tell Recorder says DVR, XVR, "Turbo HD", "HDCVI" or "AHD" Recorder says NVR; cameras use LAN cables

docs.title: Step 2: Choose the upgrade route
docs.text:
Route What we do Good Watch out A. AI DVR / XVR (analog) Replace only the old DVR with an AI DVR/XVR Cheapest, no new cabling Usually basic AI, often on some channels only B. AI NVR (IP) Replace only the NVR with an AI NVR Keeps all IP cameras With mixed brands (ONVIF), AI may be limited. Test before promising C. AI box Add a separate AI device that reads existing video Nothing replaced; good for mixed setups Extra device; needs IP video streams D. Replace key cameras AI cameras (ideally with siren and light) at 2–4 key spots Best value; combines with A or B Only covers the key spots

ONVIF is a common "language" that lets cameras and recorders from different brands work together. Recording usually works across brands, but AI features may not.

docs.title: Which route to choose
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Q1{"Cameras working and<br/>image quality OK?"}
    Q1 -- No --> R0["Replace bad cameras<br/>+ AI cameras at key spots"]
    Q1 -- Yes --> Q2{Analog or IP?}
    Q2 -- Analog --> A["Route A: AI DVR/XVR<br/>+ Route D for key spots"]
    Q2 -- IP --> Q3{"Same brand as the<br/>new AI NVR?"}
    Q3 -- Yes --> B[Route B: AI NVR]
    Q3 -- "No / mixed" --> C["Route C: AI box,<br/>or test ONVIF first"]

docs.title: Step 3: Check image quality first
docs.text:
AI is only as good as what the camera sees. If a camera's image is poor, replace that camera.

Problem Result Very old, low-resolution camera People look blurry, AI misses them Weak or dead night vision (IR) Dark images at night Dirty, scratched or foggy lens Blur and false alarms Bad angle (too high, facing the sun) AI can't recognise people

docs.title: Site survey checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Analog (DVR) or IP (NVR)?
  • [ ] Recorder brand, model and age
  • [ ] Number of cameras, brand and resolution
  • [ ] Image quality in the day and at night, for each camera
  • [ ] Cameras in the right places for AI (gate, wall, entrance)?
  • [ ] Hard disk health and recording days
  • [ ] What does the customer actually want? (Night intrusion, gate log, footfall)
  • [ ] Internet available? (Only needed for phone alerts or cloud)

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Promising full AI on a mixed-brand system without testing.
  • Ignoring poor night vision on old cameras, then blaming the AI.
  • Quoting a full replacement when an upgrade would do. The customer says no.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A factory had 16 analog cameras and an 8-year-old DVR, and wanted night intrusion alerts. The survey found 14 cameras with good images and 2 boundary cameras with dead night vision.

Option What Result Replace everything 16 new AI cameras + new NVR + cabling Too expensive; the owner said no AI XVR only New AI XVR, keep all 16 cameras Doesn't work: the 2 boundary cameras show black images at night, so the AI can't detect anyone there Smart upgrade New AI XVR + replace the 2 boundary cameras with cameras that have working night vision + keep 14 Night alerts work at a fraction of the cost; AMC signed Optional add-on Make those 2 replacement cameras ones with siren and light Also scares intruders away, for a small extra cost

Why not just the AI XVR? AI can't detect what the camera can't see. Upgrade the recorder first, replace only the cameras that can't see properly, and offer deterrence (siren and light) as an optional upsell, not a must.

docs.title: Business opportunity
docs.text:
1. Take the list of past customers.
  2. Offer a free "AI upgrade check" (site survey).
  3. Use the checklist and quote an upgrade route.
  4. Add an AMC to every upgrade.

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "You don't need to throw away your cameras. We'll check them, replace only the recorder or a couple of key cameras, and you'll get smart alerts on your phone for people and vehicles at a much lower cost."

docs.title: Camera placement for AI
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-11

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: AI needs to see the target big enough, from the right angle, in good light. Most "AI doesn't work" complaints are really placement problems.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: Correct placement is the difference between reliable alerts and missed intruders or constant false alarms, even with the best camera.

docs.title: 1. Height and angle
docs.text:
TOO HIGH (8m+)             RIGHT (about 2.5–4m)          TOO LOW (under 2m)
        📷                           📷
        │                             ╲
        │ looks straight              ╲  sees people          📷──── easy to hit,
        │ down → only                  ╲ from the side           block or turn
        ▼ heads visible          🧍     ╲→ full body
       🧍                                                     🧍
Placement Problem Too high Sees only heads and shoulders; AI can't recognise a person Too low Easy to vandalise, cover or turn; passing people block the view Right About 2.5–4 m (check the install guide), tilted down a little so people appear full body, from the side or front
  • Keep sky out of the picture, or only a small strip.
  • Point the camera along the area people walk through, not straight across it at close range.

docs.title: 2. Distance and size on screen (DORI)
docs.text:
The further away a person is, the smaller they look. Pixels per metre measures how much detail the camera captures. The DORI standard:

Level Pixels per metre What you can do Needed for Detect 25 See that someone is there Intrusion, line-crossing Observe 62 See clothing, actions Smart search by colour Recognise 125 Recognise a known person Checking footage of staff Identify 250 Identify a stranger beyond doubt Face recognition, ANPR

Spec sheets list DORI distances for each camera. They're "up to" figures, so plan for less.

docs.title: Lens choice
docs.text: Lens Sees Best for Wide (e.g. 2.8 mm) Wide area, short distance Rooms, shopfronts, small yards Narrow (e.g. 6 mm, 8 mm) Narrow area, further Long walls, driveways, far gates Varifocal / motorised zoom Adjustable at installation Fine-tuning AI coverage

docs.title: 3. Light
docs.text: Problem Fix Facing the sun or bright gates Change the angle; use WDR cameras Headlights shining into the lens Angle away from the road; use ANPR cameras at gates Area beyond the IR range Longer IR range, add a light, or colour night vision IR reflection (camera too close to a wall, roof edge or pole) Mount away from surfaces; clean spider webs regularly

docs.title: 4. Drawing zones and lines
docs.text:
• Draw lines where the person appears full body, not at the edge of the picture.
  • Include the approach area in intrusion zones, not just the wall.
  • Leave out trees, roads and areas outside the property.
  • Overlap coverage at corners.

docs.title: 5. Obstacles
docs.text:
• Trees and plants grow and can block the view in months.
  • Parked vehicles, stacked goods, poles and signboards.
  • Moving things in the zone: flags, banners, fans.

docs.title: Placement by feature
docs.text: Feature Height Distance Key tip Intrusion / line-crossing About 2.5–4 m Within detect range Full body visible; keep sky out Face recognition About head height (slightly above) Close: identify range Narrow entry point; avoid backlight ANPR Low to medium, facing the plate Close: identify range Slow vehicles, small angle, 1 lane People counting Ceiling, looking down Above the entrance Dedicated overhead camera Smart search About 2.5–4 m Within observe range Clear view of clothing colours

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• One wide camera trying to cover a long wall.
  • Mounting too high "to see everything."
  • Ignoring the IR range at the far end of the scene.
  • Camera mounted right under a roof edge, causing IR reflection.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A warehouse used one wide (2.8 mm) camera at a corner to cover a 60 m wall. At the far end, people were too small to detect, and it was beyond the IR range at night. The fix: 2 cameras, one at each end, each covering half the wall with a narrower lens and enough IR range. The whole wall was then covered day and night.

docs.title: Placement checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Height about 2.5–4 m (or as per feature)
  • [ ] People visible full body, from the side or front
  • [ ] Target within the camera's DORI range for the feature
  • [ ] Right lens for the distance
  • [ ] Not facing the sun or headlights; little or no sky
  • [ ] Within IR range at night; away from walls, roofs and webs
  • [ ] Zones and lines drawn properly; trees and roads left out
  • [ ] No obstacles; corners overlap

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "Where we put the camera matters as much as which camera we use. We'll place each one at the right height and distance so the AI clearly sees people coming, day and night. That's why we do a site visit before quoting."

docs.title: Testing a demo setup
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-11

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: Set up one AI demo at the shop, test it honestly for 7 days, log every result, and use it for a 5-minute live customer demo that ends with one honest limit.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: Customers believe what they see. A live demo, backed by our own test results, is more convincing than any brochure, and it stops us overpromising.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Item Why Tip 1 AI camera, ideally with siren and light Shows detection and deterrence Entry AI tier is fine 1 normal camera Compare normal motion alerts vs AI Side-by-side is the most convincing demo AI NVR (same brand as the AI camera) Recording, smart search, AI on the normal camera Same brand = all features work PoE switch + hard disk Power, network, recording Ask the distributor for a demo unit Phone with the brand's app Show live alerts Turn off battery saver for the app

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• One camera outside (entrance or side lane), one inside (shop floor or counter).
  • Follow the placement checklist.
  • Turn on human/vehicle detection, line-crossing, an intrusion zone, loitering, a schedule, phone alerts, siren and light.
  • Save a backup of the settings.

docs.title: 7-day test plan
docs.text: Day What to test 1 Walk across the line at normal speed, slowly, fast; groups of 2–3 2 Tricky walks: crouch or crawl, carry a big box, umbrella, helmet 3 Distance: 5 m, 10 m, 15 m, 20 m+. Where does detection stop? 4 Vehicles: bike, car, cycle. Correct classification? 5 Night: repeat Days 1–3 in the dark; check IR range and siren 6 False alarm sources: animals, trees, plastic bags, headlights, rain 7 Compare 24-hour alert counts (normal vs AI camera); test smart search

docs.title: Test log template
docs.text:
Date Time Day/Night Test Expected Result Notes Walk across line at 10 m Alert Crouch across line Alert Dog in zone No alert

Count at the end:

  • Correct alerts: real person or vehicle, alert sent
  • False alarms: alert, but no real person or vehicle
  • Missed events: real person or vehicle, no alert

Add the findings to this knowledge base, e.g. the real detection distance at night for the model tested.

docs.title: 5-minute customer demo
docs.text: Step What you do What the customer sees What you say 1 Show live view with AI boxes Boxes around people and vehicles only "It knows a person from a dog or a tree." 2 A colleague walks across the line Siren, light, and a phone alert in seconds "This is what an intruder would get." 3 Show the 24-hour alert counts Normal camera: many alerts; AI camera: a few, all real "Which alerts would you trust?" 4 Smart search: "person, red top, last hour" Results in seconds "No more watching hours of video." 5 Tell them one honest limit n/a "At night it works well up to about X m, so for your long wall we'd use 2 cameras."

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Testing only in the daytime.
  • Not writing down failures. Failures are the most valuable results.
  • Demo phone with battery saver on, so the alert doesn't arrive during the demo.
  • Promising results from the brochure instead of our own tests.

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "We tested this ourselves for a week, day and night. Let me show you how it works live, and also where its limits are, so we design your system properly."

docs.title: Reading a spec sheet
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-10

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: Don't trust "AI" in the product name. Read the smart features section of the spec sheet: real AI says "deep learning" or "human/vehicle classification."

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: It stops us selling a product that won't do what the customer needs, and it explains why our price is higher than cheap "AI" cameras online.

docs.title: What's in a spec sheet
docs.text: Section What it tells you Look for Camera Image quality Resolution, lens, night vision range Smart / AI features ("Smart event", "Deep learning", "VCA") What AI it actually does The most important section Video Recording format H.265 Network Compatibility ONVIF Interface Extra hardware Built-in speaker, light, alarm input/output General Build and power IP67, PoE, operating temperature

docs.title: Real AI vs marketing label
Traps in the small print
docs.text: Trap What it really means "Supported with compatible NVR" Works only with that brand's AI NVR "Face capture" Only takes face photos; recognition needs an AI NVR or software Recorder: "AI: 4-ch", "Perimeter protection: 8-ch" AI works on only that many cameras "Up to" distances Ideal conditions; plan for less "Requires license" Extra payment to unlock the feature ANPR "speed ≤ X km/h", "angle ≤ X°" Plates are read only within these conditions

docs.title: Example: two cameras sold as "AI"
docs.text: Camera A: "AI Smart Camera" Camera B: "4MP Bullet Camera" Smart features listed Smart motion detection, line crossing, intrusion, tampering Deep learning: human and vehicle classification, line crossing and intrusion (human/vehicle), false alarm filtering Actually AI? Probably not: no classification Yes At a site with trees and dogs Many false alarms Few false alarms

docs.title: Other specs worth knowing
docs.text: Spec Simple meaning Why it matters IR range How far night vision reaches AI can't detect beyond it at night Colour night vision Colour video at night using light Easier to identify clothes and vehicles WDR Handles bright and dark areas together Doorways with sunlight behind people H.265 Video compression Saves hard disk space IP67 Dust- and water-proof Outdoor cameras IK10 Vandal-proof Low-mounted or public places Built-in speaker / light Warnings and flashing Active deterrence

docs.title: The 6-question check
docs.text:
• [ ] Says human/vehicle classification or deep learning?
  • [ ] Which AI features exactly?
  • [ ] Works alone, or only with a compatible NVR?
  • [ ] Recorders: how many channels get AI?
  • [ ] Any extra licence needed?
  • [ ] Night vision range enough for the site?

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A customer asked why our AI camera costs more than an "AI camera" online. The online camera's spec sheet listed smart motion detection with no classification. Ours listed deep learning, human/vehicle classification, false alarm filtering and a built-in siren. Showing both spec sheets justified the price.

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "Many cheap cameras just put an 'AI' sticker on normal motion detection, so trees and dogs keep setting them off. Ours actually recognises people and vehicles. You'll get alerts you can trust. I can show you both spec sheets."

docs.title: Handling customer objections
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-11

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: An objection is a question in disguise. Listen, agree with the feeling, ask for the real reason, answer simply with proof, check, and always end with a small next step.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: Answering concerns honestly, with proof, helps customers make a confident decision, and helps us win the sale without cutting the price.

docs.title: The 5-step method
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["1. Listen<br/>don't interrupt"] --> B["2. Agree<br/>with the feeling"]
    B --> C["3. Ask<br/>the real reason"]
    C --> D["4. Answer<br/>+ proof"]
    D --> E["5. Check<br/>'Does that help?'"]
    E --> F["Next step:<br/>survey, demo, quote"]

Proof beats talk: the live demo, spec sheets, our test log, the payback calculation, real examples.

docs.title: Money objections
docs.text: Objection What they really mean Answer Proof "Too expensive." "I don't see the value yet" "What does a night guard or one theft cost you? This pays for itself in about X months." Then offer Basic Payback calculation, 3 packages "Online is cheaper." "Why pay more for the same thing?" "Many cheap ones are normal motion detection with an 'AI' sticker. Ours includes setup, AI tuning and local service." Two spec sheets side by side "Why pay for AMC every year?" "Will I get anything for it?" "AI cameras need tuning, cleaning and updates. We visit every 3 months, so it works when you need it." AMC checklist

docs.title: "We don't need it" objections

You can keep your cameras; we just upgrade the brain." Upgrade routes "Motion detection is enough." "I don't see the difference" "How many motion alerts do you get at night? docs.title: Pricing, packages and AMC
docs.text:
Draft

Last updated: 2026-10-11

Use real prices

Prices vary by brand, city and distributor. Numbers on this page are examples only. Use the distributor's price list and our current rates.

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: Price = hardware + installation + AI setup and tuning (never free) + AMC + add-ons. Justify with payback, always offer 3 packages, and push AMC for recurring income.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: Clear packages make choosing easy, the payback calculation shows the value, and AMC keeps the system working.

docs.title: What goes into the price
docs.text:
Part Includes Note Hardware Cameras, recorder, hard disk, PoE switch, cables, mounts, UPS Distributor price + margin Installation Cabling, mounting, testing Per camera or per job AI setup and tuning Zones, lines, schedules, sensitivity, alerts, app, 2-week fine-tuning Never free; it's our expertise AMC Yearly maintenance and support Recurring income Add-ons Siren/light upgrade, boom barrier, cloud subscription, extra storage Upsells

The list of all items in a quote is the BOM (Bill of Materials).

docs.title: Setting the price
docs.text:
Cost-plus: price = cost + margin. Count every cost: travel, wasted cable, extra visits.

Value-based: compare with what the customer saves or avoids losing: a night guard's salary, the cost of one theft, hours spent searching footage.

Payback period (months) = System price ÷ Monthly saving or loss avoided

Example only: a ₹60,000 system that avoids ₹10,000 a month of theft or guard cost pays for itself in 6 months.

docs.title: Packages: Good, Better, Best
docs.text:
Example: a warehouse with 8 existing cameras.

Basic Standard (recommended) Premium AI recorder (keep existing cameras) Yes Yes Yes AI alerts: intrusion, line-crossing Yes Yes Yes New AI cameras with siren and light No 2 cameras 4 cameras ANPR at the gate No No Yes AI setup + 2-week tuning Yes Yes Yes AMC Optional 1 year included 1 year comprehensive Price ₹____ ₹____ ₹____
  • Standard should truly solve the main problem. Mark it "Recommended."
  • Premium makes Standard look reasonable.
  • Basic keeps price-sensitive customers from walking away.

docs.title: AMC
docs.text:
Non-comprehensive AMC Comprehensive AMC Covers Service visits + labour Service + labour + replacement parts Parts Charged extra Included (with limits) Price Lower Higher Best for Small customers Businesses that want no surprises

What an AI AMC includes:

  • Quarterly visits: clean lenses, remove webs, check angles
  • AI re-tuning: sensitivity, zones, schedules, season changes
  • Firmware updates every 6 months
  • Hard disk and UPS health checks
  • App and alert support
  • Priority response (e.g. within 24–48 hours)

AMC pricing: often a percentage of system value per year, or a fixed fee per camera. Use our current AMC rates as the base, plus a little for AI tuning.

timeline
    Year 1 : Sale + installation + AMC
    Year 2 : AMC renewal
    Year 3 : AMC renewal : Upgrade opportunity
    Year 4+ : AMC renewal : Referrals

docs.title: Discounts
docs.text: Don't Do Cut the price straight away Remove items (Standard → Basic) Give a free AMC Discount AMC when prepaid for 2–3 years Discount AI setup and tuning Add a small add-on (extra hard disk, mount) Match the online price Show the value: setup, tuning, service, local support

docs.title: What a good quote includes
docs.text:
1. Customer name, site, date
  2. The problem we're solving, in their words
  3. 3 packages side by side, with Recommended marked
  4. BOM for each package
  5. Installation and AI setup/tuning shown separately
  6. AMC options
  7. Warranty: brand product warranty vs our service
  8. Payment terms and quote validity (e.g. 15 days)

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Giving AI setup and tuning away free.
  • Quoting one line ("8 cameras + NVR: ₹X") with no explanation.
  • Offering AMC as an afterthought, or free.
  • Cutting price instead of removing items.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A godown owner compared a one-line competitor quote with ours: 3 packages, the problem stated, AI tuning shown, a payback calculation and AMC with quarterly visits. Our Standard package cost a bit more, but the owner chose us because he understood the value and trusted the service.

docs.text: "Here are three options. Standard solves your main problem and is what I'd recommend. It pays for itself in a few months, and our AMC keeps it tuned and working every year."

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: Start with the customer's pain, not the product. Ask 5 questions, then match AI features to the customer type.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: Customers buy solutions to their problems, not "AI features." Matching the right features to their pain makes the offer relevant and easier to say yes to.

docs.title: 5 questions to ask every customer
docs.text:
1. What are you most worried about? (Theft, staff, safety, visitors?)
  2. When does it happen? (Night, closing time, busy hours?)
  3. Where? (Gate, wall, counter, godown, parking?)
  4. Do you have cameras already? (Upgrade or new?)
  5. Who will watch the alerts? (Owner, guard, manager?)
flowchart LR
    A[Ask the 5 questions] --> B[Find the main pain]
    B --> C[Match AI features]
    C --> D{Cameras already?}
    D -- Yes --> E[Upgrade proposal]
    D -- No --> F[New install proposal]
    E --> G[Add AMC]
    F --> G

docs.title: Who needs what
docs.text: Customer Main pain Key AI features Retail shop / showroom Theft, knowing customer numbers Intrusion (night), people counting, smart search Jewellery shop High-value theft, known shoplifters Face recognition (block list, VIP), loitering outside, intrusion + siren Warehouse / godown Night theft, truck movements Line-crossing on walls, intrusion, siren and light, ANPR at gate Factory Theft, worker safety, gate control Perimeter AI, ANPR for trucks, face attendance, PPE detection Housing society Unknown visitors, vehicle entry ANPR + boom barrier, face at pedestrian gate, loitering, smart search School / college Child safety, outsiders Intrusion after hours, face at gates (with consent), loitering near gates Hospital / clinic Crowds, theft, restricted areas Occupancy, intrusion in restricted rooms, ANPR parking, smart search Office Access, attendance, after-hours entry Face attendance and access, intrusion after hours Restaurant / café Footfall, kitchen and cash theft People counting, queue alerts, intrusion after hours, smart search Petrol pump Night theft, vehicle disputes ANPR, intrusion at night, smart search Construction site Material theft, no power or internet Intrusion + siren, solar or 4G cameras Home / farmhouse Break-ins when away Intrusion + siren and light, stranger alert, phone alerts

docs.title: The 4 biggest opportunities
docs.text:
Customer Solution Pitch Warehouse / godown Line-crossing on walls, intrusion in the yard at night, siren and light cameras, ANPR at the gate "Stop thieves before they take anything, and know every truck that came in and out." Housing society ANPR + boom barrier, visitor logging, face camera at the pedestrian gate, loitering near the boundary "Residents' cars enter automatically, every visitor is recorded, and no paper register." Retail shop / showroom People counting + conversion rate, intrusion after closing, smart search "Know how many customers walk in, how many buy, and find any incident in minutes." Factory Perimeter AI, ANPR for trucks, face attendance, PPE detection (check availability) "Secure the boundary, track every truck, and check workers wear safety gear."

Housing societies decide by committee (slower), but one decision means a big order plus AMC.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
Priority Who Why 1 Existing customers Already trust us; offer an upgrade 2 Warehouses, godowns, factories Clear pain, easy to show value, bigger orders 3 Housing societies Big orders + ANPR + AMC; slower decisions 4 Retail shops and showrooms Many of them; people counting is a fresh angle

Focus on 2–3 customer types and become known for them, e.g. "the AI security experts for warehouses in our area."

docs.title: Be careful with
docs.text: Situation Why Face recognition in schools or public places Privacy and legal risk (DPDP); needs consent and legal advice Promising crime prevention AI reduces risk but can't guarantee anything. Say "warns and deters" Advanced features (PPE, sentence search) Check product support and test first

Proposal: AI XVR (keep 12 cameras), 2 siren-and-light AI cameras on the back wall, line-crossing and intrusion at night, alerts to the owner and guard, and AMC. The owner also referred a friend who is secretary of a housing society.

docs.title: In one line
docs.text: Most AI complaints aren't AI problems. Check in order: what the camera sees, the settings, the recorder, alert delivery to the phone, and only then the AI.

docs.title: Why it matters to the customer
docs.text: Fast, correct fixes keep customers happy and trusting AI CCTV. Regular maintenance prevents most problems.

docs.title: Troubleshooting order
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["1. Live view, day and night:<br/>can a human clearly see the person?"] -- No --> A1["Camera, placement<br/>or light problem"]
    A -- Yes --> B["2. Settings: AI on, zone, line,<br/>direction, sensitivity, schedule"]
    B --> C["3. Recorder: AI channel limit,<br/>hard disk, date/time, firmware"]
    C --> D["4. Alert delivery: internet,<br/>app notifications, phone battery saver"]
    D --> E["5. Only then suspect the AI<br/>(contact distributor)"]

docs.title: "Too many false alarms"
docs.text: Likely cause Fix Sensitivity too high Lower it a little and test Zone includes trees, roads or neighbours Redraw the zone to cover only the property Spider webs or insects near the lens Clean regularly Rain drops on the lens Sunshade or hood; angle slightly down No schedule Alerts only for closed hours Plain motion detection on instead of AI Switch to human/vehicle detection Shadows, headlights or reflections Change the angle; remove the area from the zone

docs.title: "It missed someone"
docs.text: Likely cause Fix Person too far or small Check DORI range; add a camera or narrower lens Camera too high Lower to about 2.5–4 m Sensitivity too low Raise it a little and test Line at the edge of the picture Redraw where the person is full body Wrong line direction Set the direction to match the threat Outside the schedule Check schedule hours and recorder date/time AI off on that channel (channel limit) Move AI to the important cameras

docs.title: "Night is bad"
docs.text: Likely cause Fix Beyond the IR range Longer IR range, extra light, or colour night vision IR reflection Move away from walls and roof edges IR LEDs failed Replace the camera Headlight or streetlight glare Change the angle; WDR camera

docs.title: "Alerts aren't reaching my phone"
docs.text:
The most common complaint, and often the AI is working fine.

Likely cause Fix Phone battery saver stops the app (common on Xiaomi, Vivo, Oppo, Realme and others) Allow background running; turn off battery optimisation for the app App notifications off Turn on in the app and phone settings Internet down at the site Check the router (recording continues locally) Power cut UPS for recorder, router and PoE switch Event not set to "notify" Turn on app/cloud notification for that event Logged out or new phone Log in again; re-enable notifications

docs.title: "It suddenly stopped working"
docs.text: Likely cause Fix Settings changed or reset Re-check AI settings; keep a settings backup after installation Camera moved Re-aim and tighten the mount Hard disk failed or full Check disk health; replace Old firmware Update from the brand or distributor Wrong date and time Set the time zone and time sync

docs.title: "Face or plate reading is wrong"
docs.text: Likely cause Fix Face: bad angle, backlight, masks, poor enrolment photos See Face recognition ANPR: speed, angle, dirty or fancy plates, glare See ANPR

docs.title: Maintenance (AMC)
docs.text: When What First 1–2 weeks after installation Review alerts with the customer; fine-tune sensitivity and zones Every 3 months Clean lenses, remove webs, check angles, trim trees, check disk health Every 6 months Update firmware, check UPS battery, review schedules Season change Winter sun sits lower (new glare); monsoon brings rain and insects. Re-check angles

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A restaurant owner complained of no alerts for 3 days. The live view was clear, settings were correct, and the recorder log showed alerts were triggered. The real cause: a new phone whose battery saver blocked the app. Fixed in 2 minutes.

docs.title: How to explain it to a customer
docs.text: "AI cameras need some tuning and care, like any machine. In the first two weeks we fine-tune them for your site, and our AMC keeps them clean, updated and working properly."
